## What you should be able to do after this week

1. Say why project management became a mainstream skill rather than a construction speciality.
2. Apply the temporary-and-unique test, and name the cases where it returns an unhelpful answer.
3. Distinguish a project from a program and from a portfolio, and say what changes at each step.
4. Describe the four stages of the project life cycle and how effort is distributed across them.
5. Say what makes a project unsuitable for up-front planning, and what agile does about it.
6. Separate the technical and sociocultural dimensions of the work, and explain why competence in one does not substitute for the other.

## 1 · Why this is a mainstream skill

Project management used to be the property of construction, defence contracting and film production. It is now the ordinary way a large amount of work gets done, in the private sector and outside it — emergency aid after a natural disaster, a crime-reduction strategy, the renovation of a public playground.

Two numbers give the scale. Roughly **$2.5 trillion**, about a quarter of US gross national product, is spent on projects each year. And membership of the Project Management Institute grew from **93,000 in 2002 to more than 686,000 in 2021** — a sevenfold increase in under two decades [1].

The more useful observation is quieter: **most people who manage projects never hold the title.** Accountants running an audit, lawyers running a case, teachers coaching a debate team, a store manager building a retention programme, a clinician organising a community health event. For these people project management is not a job title but a job requirement. With three to four career changes now typical, the skill travels better than almost any other you will acquire [1].

That is the argument for taking this seriously even if you never intend to be a project manager.

## 2 · What a project is

The Project Management Institute's definition is the one to memorise:

> A project is a temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result.

Two words carry the weight. **Temporary** means a definite beginning and end — bounded, not necessarily brief. **Unique** means not previously produced in this exact configuration.

Larson and Gray expand this into five characteristics [1]:

| # | Characteristic | What it rules out |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | An established objective | Open-ended work with no definition of done |
| 2 | A defined lifespan, with a beginning and an end | Ongoing operational responsibility |
| 3 | Usually involves several departments and professions | Work a single function can absorb alone |
| 4 | Typically doing something not done before | Pure repetition |
| 5 | Specific time, cost and performance requirements | Work nobody is measuring |

: {tbl-colwidths="[6,40,54]"}

The fifth deserves attention. Those three requirements — time, cost, performance — are the **triple constraint**, and they impose a level of accountability that ordinary work rarely carries. Balancing the trade-offs among them, while still satisfying the customer, is one of the primary functions of the role.

The fourth is a matter of degree rather than a clean test. Landing a rover on Mars requires solving genuinely unsolved problems. A routine commercial fit-out uses established procedures throughout — and is still customised enough to count.

### What a project is not

A project is not routine, repetitive work. Daily work does the same or similar thing repeatedly; a project is done once and leaves something new behind.

| Routine, repetitive work | Project |
|:--|:--|
| Taking lecture notes each week | Writing the term paper |
| Posting invoices to the ledger | Standing up a new billing system |
| Answering supply-chain queries | Building the supply-chain dashboard those queries revealed a need for |
| Running the weekly sprint ceremonies | Migrating the team off the legacy repository |
| Servicing machines on a maintenance rota | Commissioning the replacement line |

: {tbl-colwidths="[46,54]"}

The distinction matters for a practical reason: resources consumed by daily operations are resources not spent on the innovative work that carries the organisation forward. Organisations that cannot tell the two apart tend to starve the second.

### The boundary is a management choice

Some cases resist the test, and they are the interesting ones.

- **A film production.** Temporary and unique — but the studio makes one every year.
- **A software release train.** Each release is unique; the cadence is thoroughly operational.
- **A refinery maintenance shutdown.** Recurring on a fixed cycle, yet planned and run as a project every time.

So "project vs. operation" is a decision about **which toolkit to apply**, not a fact about the world. The refinery treats the shutdown as a project because project controls give better answers than operational ones, not because the universe classified it that way.

### Project, program, portfolio

The terms are routinely used as synonyms. They are not.

| Term | Definition | What changes |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Project** | A temporary endeavour producing a unique output | The unit of delivery |
| **Program** | A group of related projects pursuing a common goal over an extended period | Scale and time span; each project keeps its own manager, and program goals tie closely to broad strategic objectives |
| **Portfolio** | The set of projects and programs an organisation chooses to fund | Selection and prioritisation — the question stops being "how" and becomes "which" |

: {tbl-colwidths="[16,48,36]"}

A quick diagnostic: if the components have no dependencies on each other, it is a portfolio and somebody chose a more impressive word.

## 3 · The project life cycle

Projects have a limited lifespan, and the level of effort across that lifespan changes in a predictable shape. Many industries define their own phase models — a software project might use definition, design, code, integration/test, maintenance — but the generic cycle has four stages [1].

    <line x1="60" y1="252" x2="60" y2="26"/>
  </g>

    <path d="M60,252 Q152,112 244,252"/>
    <path d="M60,252 Q272,82 484,252"/>
    <path d="M182,252 Q432,14 622,252"/>
    <path d="M560,252 Q646,132 726,252"/>
  </g>
  <g font-size="14" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">
    <text x="152" y="150">Defining</text>
    <text x="272" y="120">Planning</text>
    <text x="432" y="52">Executing</text>
    <text x="646" y="170">Closing</text>
  </g>
  <g font-size="12" fill="currentColor" opacity="0.75">
    <text x="60" y="276">Start</text>
    <text x="393" y="276" text-anchor="middle">Time</text>
    <text x="726" y="276" text-anchor="end">End</text>
    <text x="30" y="140" text-anchor="middle" transform="rotate(-90 30 140)">Level of effort</text>
  </g>
</svg>
<figcaption>Effort is not evenly distributed. Executing dominates; defining is short and cheap, and is where the leverage is.</figcaption>
</figure>

| Stage | What happens | What comes out |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Defining** | Objectives set, specifications settled, teams formed, responsibilities assigned | Goals, specifications, tasks, responsibilities |
| **Planning** | Effort rises; the schedule, budget, quality level and resourcing are worked out | Schedules, budgets, resources, risks, staffing |
| **Executing** | The bulk of the work, physical and mental; progress measured against time, cost and specification | Status reports, changes, quality, forecasts |
| **Closing** | Deliver to the customer, redeploy resources, review the project | Customer training, transferred documents, released resources, evaluation, lessons learned |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,52,34]"}

Two things about closing are worth noticing, because they are the stages most often skipped. **Redeployment** is a real management task — equipment and people have to land somewhere. And the **post-project review** is where lessons become organisational rather than personal; skip it and the organisation relearns the same lesson at full price on the next project.

## 4 · When planning stops working

Traditional project management front-loads the planning, and that works precisely when the work is predictable. An engineer building a bridge draws on proven technology and established design principles: what is to be accomplished, and how, are both well understood.

Not all projects enjoy that. Uncertainty rises along two independent axes — how well the **scope** is known, and how proven the **technology** is [1].

The cost of ignoring this is documented. The Standish Group estimated that in 1995 US firms and agencies spent **$81 billion on cancelled software projects** [2]. That figure is now historical, but the problem is not: Krasner put the **cost of poor software quality in the United States at over $2 trillion in 2020**, counting unsuccessful projects, software failure and inferior legacy systems [3].

### Rolling wave

Agile project management responds with an incremental, iterative process — a **rolling wave**. Rather than planning everything up front, the design and outcome develop through a series of iterations, each typically one to four weeks.

Agile centres on close collaboration between the team and customer representatives, breaking work into small functional pieces and adapting as requirements move. It works best in **small teams of four to eight**.

**It is not an either/or.** Agile methods are often used up front to establish specifications and requirements, with traditional methods then used to plan, execute and close. They are also used on particular technical problems inside an otherwise traditional project. That blending has a name — **hybrid project management** — and it is the common case in practice, not a compromise position.

## 5 · What is driving the demand

Four forces explain why this discipline keeps expanding [1].

**Compression of the product life cycle.** In high-tech industries the product life cycle now averages six months to three years; thirty years ago ten to fifteen years was unremarkable. Time-to-market has become a competitive weapon, and the rule of thumb is unforgiving — a **six-month delay in a high-tech product can cost a third of its potential revenue share**.

**The knowledge explosion.** Products and infrastructure now integrate far more technologies than they did. Building a road was once comparatively simple; today it involves materials, specifications, codes, aesthetics, equipment and a long list of specialists. It is now hard to find a new product that does not contain at least one microchip, and increasingly hard to find one that contains no AI. Integration is the problem, and project management is the discipline that does it.

**The triple bottom line — planet, people, profit.** Sustainability moved from a public-relations concern to a design constraint. Reducing carbon and using renewable resources shows up directly in project objectives and techniques; on construction projects, achieving a LEED certification is now routinely an objective in its own right.

**Small projects, big problems.** Organisations run hundreds of projects concurrently. Small projects tend to be perceived as low-impact because they do not consume much scarce resource — yet they carry the same or more risk than large ones, and because the inefficiency of any one is small and unmeasured, it is usually invisible. In aggregate the losses are substantial and sit outside the accounting system entirely. The problem this creates is organisational: sharing and prioritising resources across a portfolio, which is where Week 2 begins.

## 6 · The socio-technical dimension

Managing projects is multidimensional, and the two dimensions are genuinely different in kind [1].

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 620 250" role="img" aria-labelledby="st-title" style="width:100%;height:auto">
  <title id="st-title">The technical and sociocultural dimensions of project management</title>
  <circle cx="238" cy="125" r="104" fill="#0F5A4B" opacity="0.14" stroke="#0F5A4B" stroke-width="1.8"/>
  <circle cx="382" cy="125" r="104" fill="currentColor" opacity="0.05" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"/>
  <text x="150" y="60" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#0F5A4B" text-anchor="middle">Technical</text>
  <text x="470" y="60" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">Sociocultural</text>
  <g font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">
    <text x="150" y="112">Scope · WBS</text>
    <text x="150" y="132">Schedules</text>
    <text x="150" y="152">Resource allocation</text>
    <text x="150" y="172">Baseline budgets</text>
    <text x="150" y="192">Status reports</text>
    <text x="470" y="112">Leadership</text>
    <text x="470" y="132">Problem solving</text>
    <text x="470" y="152">Teamwork · negotiation</text>
    <text x="470" y="172">Politics</text>
    <text x="470" y="192">Customer expectations</text>
  </g>
  <text x="310" y="130" font-size="12" font-style="italic" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" opacity="0.85">both,</text>
  <text x="310" y="148" font-size="12" font-style="italic" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" opacity="0.85">always</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>The overlap is the job. Neither dimension is a specialism you can delegate away.</figcaption>
</figure>

The **technical** dimension is the orderly one: the methodology of planning, scheduling and controlling. Scope statements link the project to the customer; the work breakdown structure serves as the database connecting every level of the organisation to every deliverable, right down to the tasks in a work package. Because those linkages are integrated, the effect of any change is documented and traceable back to its source.

The **sociocultural** dimension is the messier, often contradictory world of implementation. It means shaping a project culture that sustains teamwork and motivation, spotting and resolving problems before they threaten the work, steering back on track when — not if — things depart from plan, and building a cooperative network among stakeholders holding genuinely different standards, commitments and perspectives.

A manager must be a master of both. Competence in one does not compensate for weakness in the other, and the failure modes look nothing alike.

## 7 · Where generative AI enters

Generative AI now touches every process group. The capabilities most often claimed for it are enhanced decision making, automation, innovative solutions, content creativity, business and data modelling, personalised communication, stakeholder collaboration, scenario planning, training, continuous learning-resource optimisation, and the ethical questions that come with all of it [4].

| Process group | Where GenAI is applied | What it produces |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Initiating** | Idea generation · stakeholder engagement · requirement gathering | Project concepts from historical patterns; tailored preliminary content; requirement lists drawn from past projects |
| **Planning** | Plan drafting · risk scenario modelling · generative scenario planning | Initial plans from similar past projects; simulated risk scenarios; multiple execution scenarios |
| **Executing** | Content creation · code generation · dynamic reporting | Designs and models for project content; code snippets and modules; real-time dashboards with financial metrics |
| **Monitoring &amp; controlling** | Predictive risk narratives · feedback loops · predictive models | Descriptive risk scenarios; responses to common queries; models predicting future project states |
| **Closing** | Automated summary reports | Detailed closure reports and feedback |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20,38,42]"}

Read that table with the course's standing rule in mind. Every row describes a **generated artefact**, and a generated artefact is a claim, not a result. A model will produce a plausible, well-formatted work breakdown structure in nine seconds and quietly omit a stakeholder, because it does not know who is in your room. In this course the check is graded, not the output.

::: {.tutor}
### Tutor check — one question at a time, no lecturing

1. Define a project. Which of the five characteristics does a refinery maintenance shutdown fail, and is it still a project?
2. A vendor tells you 71% of software projects fail. What would you need to know before repeating that number?
3. Give me a program that is really a portfolio. How did you tell?
4. Effort peaks during executing, but the leverage is in defining. Explain that apparent contradiction.
5. Which of the two dimensions — technical or sociocultural — is easier to teach? Which is easier to fake?
:::

::: {.editor}
### Editor challenge — attack this claim

> "Agile is a response to bad planning. A team that understood its scope properly would not need iterations."

Attack it. Some available lines: the uncertainty figure separates scope from technology, and a team can know one and not the other; iterations buy information that no amount of up-front thinking produces; but also — the claim is not entirely wrong, since "agile in name only" is a real failure mode where ceremonies change and decision rights do not.
:::

::: {.roommate}
### Roommate link

**Cooking a dinner party vs. running a restaurant.** The dinner party is a project — fixed date, unique menu, guests who will remember it. The restaurant is operations. A chef who runs a restaurant well can still fail at a dinner party, because the failure modes differ: the restaurant's enemy is variance, the dinner party's enemy is the thing you forgot to buy.

Now notice the second lesson. You cannot cook the dinner party in iterations — the guests arrive once. That is what the uncertainty figure is telling you.
:::

## Where this sits in the course

Chapter 2 takes up how organisations evaluate and select projects; Chapter 3, the organisational environment they run in. Chapters 4 through 9 build the plan — scope and work breakdown structure, cost and time estimates, the scheduled network of activities, risk, resources and duration.

A real understanding of project management does not come from knowing what a scope statement is, or a critical path. It comes from seeing how the parts interact to determine what happens to a project.
